# 12-Week Reconditioning Programme — 3-Week Return-to-Baseline Block

**Client Profile:** Male, 41 | Intermediate lifter | Post-illness (mild flu, 3 weeks detraining) | Presenting fatigue, 4 kg bodyweight loss
**Pre-illness 1RMs:** Bench 100 kg | Squat 140 kg | Deadlift 170 kg
**Goal:** Safe, progressive return to pre-illness baseline across all three primary lifts and general conditioning

---

## Programme Philosophy

Three weeks off combined with systemic illness is not simply a detraining problem — it is a recovery problem layered on top of detraining. The fatigue and weight loss signal that the body has been in a catabolic state and the immune and endocrine systems are still normalising. Jumping back to pre-illness loads, even at 70–80%, risks injury, stalls recovery, and often produces a second energy crash in the days following the session. This block therefore prioritises **tissue re-sensitisation, movement quality, and progressive load accumulation** over ego-driven percentages.

The block runs **three training days per week** (e.g. Monday / Wednesday / Friday, or Tuesday / Thursday / Saturday). Rest days are active recovery only. Sessions should not exceed **60–65 minutes** including warm-up. If the client reports unusual fatigue, soreness, or poor sleep after any session, repeat that week's loads before advancing — there is no shame in a four-week reconditioning block.

---

## Phase Overview

| Week | Theme | Intensity Target | Volume |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Re-sensitisation & Movement Audit | 50–55% of pre-illness 1RM | Low — 2–3 sets, higher rep |
| 2 | Load Reintroduction | 60–65% | Moderate — 3–4 sets |
| 3 | Baseline Approach | 70–75% | Moderate-high — 4 sets, rep ranges tighten |

---

## Session Structure (All Three Weeks)

Every session follows the same four-part architecture:

1. **General warm-up** — 5–8 minutes of light cardio (rowing, cycling, or brisk treadmill walk). Keep heart rate below 130 bpm. This is not conditioning; it is circulation and temperature.
2. **Mobility & activation** — 8–10 minutes of targeted work (detailed per week below).
3. **Main training block** — compound lifts first, accessory work second.
4. **Cool-down** — 5 minutes of light stretching and diaphragmatic breathing. Do not skip this; parasympathetic recovery is blunted post-illness.

---

## WEEK 1 — Re-Sensitisation and Movement Audit

**Theme:** The goal this week is not to train hard. It is to move well, remind the nervous system what loaded patterns feel like, and gather information about where the client actually is. Expect him to feel stronger than the percentages suggest — that is fine. Do not chase it.

**Working loads:** Approximately 50–55% of pre-illness 1RM
- Bench: 50–55 kg
- Squat: 70–77 kg
- Deadlift: 85–93 kg

**Mobility & Activation (perform before every session this week):**
- 90/90 hip rotations — 5 reps each side
- Cat-cow — 10 reps
- Thoracic rotation in quadruped — 8 reps each side
- Glute bridges — 2 × 15
- Band pull-aparts — 2 × 20
- Goblet squat with 3-second pause at bottom — 2 × 8 with light KB (12–16 kg)

---

### Session 1A — Lower Body Focus

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Tempo | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Barbell Back Squat | 3 | 10 | 3-1-1 | 2 min |
| Romanian Deadlift | 3 | 10 | 3-1-1 | 2 min |
| Leg Press | 2 | 12 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Seated Leg Curl | 2 | 12 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Calf Raise (machine or standing) | 2 | 15 | — | 60 sec |
| Plank | 2 | 30 sec hold | — | 60 sec |

**Coaching notes:** Use the squat sets as a movement audit. Watch for any asymmetry, depth loss, or compensatory lean that wasn't present pre-illness. The Romanian deadlift is chosen over conventional this session to reintroduce hip hinge under load with a shorter range of motion and less spinal loading. Tempo is deliberate — 3 seconds down, 1-second pause, 1 second up. This is not optional.

---

### Session 1B — Upper Body Focus

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Tempo | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Barbell Bench Press | 3 | 10 | 3-1-1 | 2 min |
| Seated Cable Row | 3 | 10 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Dumbbell Overhead Press | 2 | 12 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Lat Pulldown | 2 | 12 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Dumbbell Lateral Raise | 2 | 15 | — | 60 sec |
| Face Pull | 2 | 15 | — | 60 sec |

**Coaching notes:** Bench load should feel almost embarrassingly light. That is correct. The purpose is to re-groove the movement pattern and assess shoulder health after three weeks of inactivity. If there is any shoulder discomfort, substitute dumbbell press and flag it. The pulling volume (row and pulldown) deliberately matches pressing volume — post-illness posture often deteriorates and the upper back needs attention.

---

### Session 1C — Full Body / Hinge Focus

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Tempo | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conventional Deadlift | 3 | 8 | 3-1-1 | 2.5 min |
| Goblet Squat | 2 | 12 | 3-1-1 | 90 sec |
| Dumbbell Bench Press | 3 | 10 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Single-Arm Dumbbell Row | 3 | 10 each | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Reverse Lunge | 2 | 10 each leg | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Dead Bug | 2 | 8 each side | Slow | 60 sec |

**Coaching notes:** The conventional deadlift returns here at the end of the week rather than the start. By Session 1C you will have a clearer picture of how the client is responding. Keep the deadlift crisp — if bar speed is slow or form breaks down at rep 6, stop the set. Eight quality reps at 50% is infinitely more valuable than grinding through ten poor ones. The dead bug is included specifically for post-illness core re-activation; the diaphragm and deep stabilisers are often the last things to fully recover.

---

**Week 1 Check-In Protocol:** At the end of Week 1, ask the client to rate the following on a 1–10 scale: energy levels, sleep quality, muscle soreness, and motivation. If energy and sleep are below 6, repeat Week 1 before advancing. This is not a failure — it is intelligent programming.

---

## WEEK 2 — Load Reintroduction

**Theme:** The nervous system has been reminded of the patterns. Now we begin to add meaningful load. Volume increases slightly, intensity steps up to 60–65%, and we introduce the conventional deadlift as a primary lift in its own session. The client should begin to feel like he is actually training again, but should not feel crushed after sessions.

**Working loads:** Approximately 60–65% of pre-illness 1RM
- Bench: 60–65 kg
- Squat: 84–91 kg
- Deadlift: 102–110 kg

**Mobility & Activation (perform before every session this week):**
- World's greatest stretch — 5 reps each side
- Hip flexor stretch with thoracic rotation — 5 reps each side
- Banded clamshells — 2 × 15 each side
- Band pull-aparts — 2 × 20
- Scapular push-ups — 2 × 10
- Barbell good morning (empty bar) — 2 × 10

---

### Session 2A — Lower Body / Squat Focus

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Tempo | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Barbell Back Squat | 4 | 8 | 2-1-1 | 2.5 min |
| Romanian Deadlift | 3 | 10 | 3-1-1 | 2 min |
| Walking Lunge (bodyweight or light DBs) | 3 | 10 each leg | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Leg Curl (machine) | 3 | 10 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Leg Extension | 2 | 12 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Ab Wheel Rollout | 3 | 8 | Slow | 90 sec |

**Coaching notes:** Four sets of squats at 60–65% should feel like genuine work without being a grind. If the client is moving well and bar speed is good across all four sets, make a note — he may be ready to push slightly harder in Week 3. The ab wheel rollout replaces the plank this week to increase anterior core demand progressively.

---

### Session 2B — Upper Body / Bench Focus

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Tempo | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Barbell Bench Press | 4 | 8 | 2-1-1 | 2.5 min |
| Barbell Bent-Over Row | 3 | 8 | Controlled | 2 min |
| Incline Dumbbell Press | 3 | 10 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Seated Cable Row | 3 | 10 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Overhead Press (barbell or DB) | 3 | 10 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Tricep Pushdown | 2 | 12 | — | 60 sec |
| Dumbbell Curl | 2 | 12 | — | 60 sec |

**Coaching notes:** The barbell bent-over row is introduced here as it requires more systemic demand than the cable row. Keep the back angle consistent and avoid any excessive lumbar rounding — post-illness fatigue can manifest as form breakdown in the lower back before the client is aware of it. Watch this carefully.

---

### Session 2C — Full Body / Deadlift Focus

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Tempo | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conventional Deadlift | 4 | 6 | 2-1-1 | 3 min |
| Front Squat or Goblet Squat | 3 | 8 | 2-1-1 | 2 min |
| Dumbbell Bench Press | 3 | 10 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Chest-Supported Row | 3 | 10 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Farmer's Carry | 3 | 30 metres | — | 90 sec |
| Pallof Press | 3 | 10 each side | Slow | 60 sec |

**Coaching notes:** Six reps on the deadlift at 60–65% allows the client to focus on bar path, bracing, and lockout quality without accumulating excessive fatigue. The farmer's carry is introduced here as a loaded carry is one of the best tools for rebuilding systemic resilience — it taxes the grip, core, traps, and cardiovascular system simultaneously without the spinal loading of a heavy compound lift. Start with a load that allows him to walk tall with no lateral sway.

---

**Week 2 Check-In Protocol:** Repeat the 1–10 self-assessment. Additionally, note whether the client is recovering between sessions — is he arriving to Session 2C feeling reasonably fresh, or is he still sore from 2A? If soreness is persisting beyond 48 hours, the load increase was too aggressive. Reduce Week 3 intensity by 5% and add an extra rest day if needed.

---

## WEEK 3 — Baseline Approach

**Theme:** This is the bridge week. Loads reach 70–75% of pre-illness 1RM, rep ranges tighten to reflect more strength-specific work, and the session structure begins to resemble what the client was doing before illness. By the end of this week he should feel confident, strong, and ready to re-enter his normal training programme. He will not be back at 100 kg / 140 kg / 170 kg yet — and that is fine. The goal is to arrive at the door of baseline, not to kick it down.

**Working loads:** Approximately 70–75% of pre-illness 1RM
- Bench: 70–75 kg
- Squat: 98–105 kg
- Deadlift: 119–127 kg

**Mobility & Activation (perform before every session this week):**
- Full dynamic warm-up of trainer's choice — 8 minutes
- Barbell warm-up sets: 2 × 5 at empty bar, 1 × 5 at 40–50% before working sets on all primary lifts

---

### Session 3A — Lower Body / Squat Focus

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Tempo | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Barbell Back Squat | 4 | 5 | 2-0-1 | 3 min |
| Romanian Deadlift | 3 | 8 | 3-1-1 | 2 min |
| Bulgarian Split Squat | 3 | 8 each leg | Controlled | 2 min |
| Leg Curl (machine) | 3 | 10 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Standing Calf Raise | 3 | 12 | Controlled | 60 sec |
| Ab Wheel Rollout | 3 | 10 | Slow | 90 sec |

**Coaching notes:** Five reps at 70–75% is meaningful strength work. The client should feel the weight but should not be grinding. If he completes all four sets with good bar speed and clean technique, he is on track. The Bulgarian split squat is introduced here to address any unilateral imbalances that may have developed or been exposed during the reconditioning block.

---

### Session 3B — Upper Body / Bench Focus

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Tempo | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Barbell Bench Press | 4 | 5 | 2-0-1 | 3 min |
| Barbell Bent-Over Row | 4 | 6 | Controlled | 2.5 min |
| Incline Dumbbell Press | 3 | 8 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Weighted Pull-Up or Lat Pulldown | 3 | 8 | Controlled | 2 min |
| Overhead Press | 3 | 8 | Controlled | 90 sec |
| Tricep Pushdown | 3 | 10 | — | 60 sec |
| Dumbbell Curl | 3 | 10 | — | 60 sec |

**Coaching notes:** Pull-ups return here if the client was performing them pre-illness. If bodyweight pull-ups feel heavy (which they may, given the 4 kg weight loss has partially reversed and strength is still rebuilding), use the lat pulldown or an assisted pull-up machine. Do not force it. The weighted pull-up option is there if he is moving exceptionally well.

---

### Session 3C — Full Body / Deadlift Focus

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Tempo | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conventional Deadlift | 4 | 5 | 2-1-1 | 3.5 min |
| Barbell Back Squat | 3 | 6 | 2-0-1 | 2.5 min |
| Barbell Bench Press | 3 | 6 | 2-0-1 | 2.5 min |
| Chest-Supported Row | 3 | 8 | Controlled | 2 min |
| Farmer's Carry | 3 | 40 metres | — | 90 sec |
| Pallof Press | 3 | 10 each side | Slow | 60 sec |

**Coaching notes:** Session 3C is deliberately structured as a mini full-body test — all three primary lifts appear in the same session at 70–75%. This is intentional. It gives you and the client a clear picture of where he stands across the board before transitioning to his regular programme. It is not a max-out session. It is a confident, controlled demonstration of readiness. The rest periods are generous — use them fully.

---

## Nutrition Guidance

Given the 4 kg weight loss during illness, the client is likely in a mild caloric deficit and has lost some lean tissue alongside fat and water. The nutritional priority during this block is **re-establishing a positive energy balance and supporting muscle protein synthesis**, not aggressive weight regain.

**Protein:** Target 2.0–2.2 g per kg of current bodyweight daily. If he was, say, 85 kg pre-illness and is now 81 kg, that is approximately 162–178 g of protein per day. Spread across 4–5 meals or feeding windows. This is non-negotiable during reconditioning — the muscle protein synthetic response to training is blunted post-illness and adequate protein is the primary lever to restore it.

**Calories:** Aim for a modest surplus of 200–300 kcal above maintenance. Do not push a large surplus — the digestive system is often still normalising after flu and aggressive eating can cause GI distress and further fatigue. Gradual re-feeding is more effective than trying to regain 4 kg in three weeks.

**Carbohydrates:** Prioritise carbohydrates around training sessions — a moderate carbohydrate meal or snack 60–90 minutes before training and a carbohydrate-protein combination within 60 minutes post-training. This supports glycogen replenishment and blunts the cortisol response to exercise, which is already elevated in post-illness recovery.

**Hydration:** Illness frequently leaves clients mildly chronically dehydrated. Target a minimum of 3 litres of water daily, more on training days. Electrolyte intake (sodium, potassium, magnesium) should be adequate — if the client is not eating a varied diet, a basic electrolyte supplement is reasonable.

**Supplements:** If not already using them, creatine monohydrate (3–5 g daily) is worth reintroducing or starting — it supports phosphocreatine resynthesis and has a modest but well-evidenced role in recovery. Vitamin D and zinc are worth checking if the client had a prolonged illness, as both are commonly depleted.

---

## Recovery Guidance

**Sleep:** This is the single most important recovery variable during this block. Target 7.5–9 hours per night. If the client is still experiencing fatigue, sleep is where the adaptation happens — not in the gym. If he is sleeping poorly, flag it and consider whether training volume needs to be reduced temporarily.

**Active recovery on rest days:** Light walking (20–30 minutes), swimming, or cycling at very low intensity. Nothing that elevates heart rate above 120–130 bpm. Avoid the temptation to add extra gym sessions — the three-day structure is deliberate.

**Soft tissue work:** Foam rolling and light stretching on rest days, focusing on the thoracic spine, hip flexors, and hamstrings. Post-illness muscle tissue can feel unusually stiff and dense; 10–15 minutes of soft tissue work on rest days will meaningfully improve session quality.

**Stress monitoring:** Psychological stress and physical stress draw from the same recovery pool. If the client is under significant life stress during this block, be prepared to reduce training volume rather than push through. A fatigued, stressed 41-year-old returning from illness is not the same as a fresh, rested athlete.

**Red flags — stop training and refer:** Chest tightness or palpitations during or after sessions, dizziness, persistent fever, or any return of acute illness symptoms. Post-viral fatigue can occasionally develop into something more significant; if the client is not improving week on week, a GP review is appropriate before continuing.

---

## Transition to Regular Programming

At the end of Week 3, conduct a brief informal assessment. The client does not need to test his 1RMs — that would be counterproductive. Instead, assess the following:

- Is he completing all sets and reps with good technique and reasonable bar speed?
- Is he recovering between sessions (arriving fresh, sleeping well, soreness resolving within 48 hours)?
- Is his bodyweight trending back toward pre-illness levels?
- Does he feel psychologically ready to train at normal intensity?

If the answer to all four is yes, he is ready to re-enter his pre-illness programme at approximately **80–85% of his previous working loads** in Week 4, building back to full baseline over the following two to three weeks of normal training. If any answer is no, extend the reconditioning block by one week, repeating Week 3 loads before advancing.

The 4 kg weight loss and three weeks of detraining mean he has likely lost 3–5% of his strength across the primary lifts. With good nutrition and consistent training, an intermediate lifter of his profile should expect to return to full baseline within **four to six weeks of completing this block** — well within normal physiological timelines.

# Cardio Reintegration — Week 1 (with 10k Running Background)

## The Problem With Just "Adding Cardio Back"

Three weeks off plus systemic illness does not affect running fitness linearly. Cardiovascular detraining begins within **7–10 days** of stopping, and after three weeks he will have lost a meaningful amount of aerobic efficiency — VO2max estimates suggest a 5–10% reduction over this timeframe in a trained individual. More importantly, post-viral fatigue has a specific cardiovascular signature: **heart rate at a given pace will be elevated**, sometimes significantly, compared to his pre-illness baseline. This is not fitness loss alone — it is the autonomic nervous system still recalibrating.

The 10k weekly target is achievable within this three-week block, but the route back is **time and effort-based, not distance or pace-based.** Chasing his pre-illness pace or distance in Week 1 is the single most reliable way to extend his fatigue and derail the lifting programme simultaneously.

---

## Governing Principle for All Week 1 Running

**Heart rate ceiling: 130–135 bpm throughout.**

This is non-negotiable in Week 1. If he does not have a heart rate monitor, get one on him — perceived effort is unreliable post-illness because the cardiovascular system is working harder than it feels. At 130–135 bpm he will almost certainly be running slower than his normal easy pace. He may need to walk sections. That is correct and expected, not a sign of failure.

This approach is sometimes called **Zone 2 training** — it keeps him in the aerobic base zone, avoids cortisol spikes, and allows cardiovascular adaptation without adding meaningfully to his systemic recovery burden.

---

## Week 1 Cardio Structure

Running sits on **rest days from the gym**, not on training days. In a Monday / Wednesday / Friday lifting structure, that gives Tuesday, Thursday, and the weekend as options. He needs **two runs in Week 1**, not three. The third run can wait until Week 2.

| Day | Session Type | Duration | Intensity | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rest Day 1 (e.g. Tuesday) | Easy run/walk | 20–25 min | HR ≤ 130 bpm | Run/walk as needed. No pace target. |
| Rest Day 2 (e.g. Thursday) | Easy run/walk | 25–30 min | HR ≤ 130 bpm | Slightly longer if Tuesday felt good. Still walk if HR climbs. |

**Total running volume Week 1: approximately 45–55 minutes.** Distance is irrelevant this week — do not log it, do not tell him what distance he covered until after the session. Time on feet is the metric.

---

## What to Tell Him About Pace

At his pre-illness fitness level, a 10k runner typically has an easy aerobic pace somewhere around 5:30–6:30 per kilometre depending on his ability. At 130 bpm post-illness, he may find himself at 7:00–8:00 per kilometre or slower. Some clients find this psychologically difficult — it can feel like a dramatic regression.

The reframe that tends to land well: **his heart is doing the same work at 130 bpm regardless of the pace on the watch.** The cardiovascular adaptation is happening. The pace will come back quickly once the autonomic system normalises, typically within two to three weeks of consistent Zone 2 work. Chasing pace now delays that normalisation.

---

## Week 1 Running Warm-Up and Cool-Down

Do not skip these — post-illness connective tissue and muscle temperature regulation are both slightly impaired.

**Before each run (5 minutes):**
- Brisk walk — 2 minutes
- Leg swings front to back — 10 each leg
- Leg swings side to side — 10 each leg
- Hip circles — 8 each direction
- Ankle rotations — 10 each
- 30-second very light jog to confirm HR response before settling into pace

**After each run (5 minutes):**
- Walk — 2 minutes
- Standing quad stretch — 30 seconds each side
- Standing calf stretch — 30 seconds each side
- Seated hamstring stretch — 30 seconds each side
- Diaphragmatic breathing — 10 slow breaths

---

## Red Flags Specific to Running Post-Illness

Running is more cardiovascularly demanding than lifting and will expose post-viral cardiac stress more readily. Stop the run and do not continue that session if he experiences any of the following:

- Heart rate that will not come down below 140 bpm despite slowing to a walk
- Dizziness or lightheadedness at any point
- Chest tightness or unusual breathlessness disproportionate to effort
- Heart rate that spikes suddenly without change in pace
- Feeling significantly worse 24 hours after a run than before it

The last point is particularly important. **Post-exertional malaise** — feeling worse the day after exercise rather than better — is a key indicator that the volume or intensity is too high for current recovery status. If he reports this after either run, drop to walking only for the remainder of Week 1 and reassess.

---

## Progression Across the Three Weeks

So he can see where this is heading:

| Week | Runs Per Week | Duration Per Run | Intensity | Approx Distance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 20–30 min | HR ≤ 130 bpm | 3–4 km per run |
| 2 | 2–3 | 30–35 min | HR ≤ 135 bpm, short pickups permitted | 4–5 km per run |
| 3 | 3 | 35–45 min | HR ≤ 140 bpm, one run with 10-min tempo section | 5–7 km per run |

By the end of Week 3 he should be completing a single run of 35–45 minutes comfortably, with one of the three runs including a controlled tempo section. A full 10k at something approaching his pre-illness pace is a **Week 4–5 target**, not a Week 3 target. Trying to compress that timeline is the most common mistake returning runners make.

# Nutrition During Reconditioning — Target Intake

## What We're Working With

Before building the numbers, it's worth being explicit about what has actually happened physiologically. The 4 kg loss over three weeks of illness is unlikely to be purely fat. In a male intermediate lifter, that kind of acute weight loss typically breaks down roughly as follows:

- **Glycogen and associated water:** 1.0–1.5 kg. Muscle glycogen stores drop rapidly during illness due to reduced carbohydrate intake and elevated inflammatory cytokines. Each gram of glycogen holds approximately 3 g of water, so glycogen depletion accounts for a disproportionate share of scale weight loss.
- **Lean tissue:** 0.8–1.5 kg. Three weeks of inactivity combined with reduced protein intake and elevated cortisol during illness creates a catabolic environment. Some lean tissue loss is almost certain.
- **Fat mass:** 0.5–1.0 kg. Illness suppresses appetite and elevates metabolic rate slightly, so some fat loss will have occurred, but it is the smallest component of the total.
- **Residual dehydration:** 0.5–1.0 kg. Chronic mild dehydration post-illness is common and often persists longer than people realise.

This breakdown matters for nutrition strategy because **glycogen and water come back quickly with adequate carbohydrate intake and hydration — within one to two weeks.** Lean tissue takes longer and requires consistent protein intake and progressive training stimulus. Fat mass is not a priority either way. The practical implication is that he will likely see 1.5–2 kg return to the scale within the first week or two simply from rehydration and glycogen replenishment, and should not interpret that as fat gain.

---

## Establishing His Numbers

We do not have his exact current bodyweight stated, so the calculations below use a working assumption. **Adjust these figures proportionally if his actual weight differs.**

**Assumed pre-illness bodyweight:** 85 kg
**Assumed current bodyweight:** 81 kg
**Target bodyweight for calculations:** Use **current bodyweight (81 kg)** for all calculations during reconditioning. Do not calculate off his pre-illness weight — that inflates targets beyond what his current system can efficiently use.

---

## Step 1 — Estimated Maintenance Calories

For an intermediate male lifter aged 41, training three days per week with two runs, a reasonable TDEE estimate uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation as a base and applies an activity multiplier.

**Basal Metabolic Rate (Mifflin-St Jeor):**
We need height for precision, but using population averages for a 41-year-old male at 81 kg and approximately 178 cm:

> BMR = (10 × 81) + (6.25 × 178) − (5 × 41) + 5
> BMR = 810 + 1112.5 − 205 + 5
> **BMR ≈ 1,722 kcal**

**Activity multiplier:**
During reconditioning Week 1 — three moderate gym sessions and two easy runs — he sits at a **lightly to moderately active** level. Use a multiplier of **1.55**, which reflects structured exercise five days per week at low-to-moderate intensity.

> TDEE = 1,722 × 1.55
> **TDEE ≈ 2,669 kcal**

Round to **2,650–2,700 kcal as estimated maintenance.**

**Important caveat:** Post-illness metabolic rate can be slightly elevated for one to two weeks as the immune system completes its work, and appetite regulation hormones (ghrelin and leptin in particular) are often disrupted. These numbers are a starting framework, not a precise prescription. Track bodyweight across the week and adjust accordingly.

---

## Step 2 — Caloric Target

The programme previously recommended a surplus of 200–300 kcal above maintenance. That remains the right approach, but it is worth explaining the reasoning in more detail so the client understands why a larger surplus is not better.

**Why not a larger surplus?**

Post-illness digestive function is often compromised — gut motility, enzyme production, and microbiome composition can all be transiently disrupted. Pushing 500+ kcal above maintenance in this state frequently results in bloating, GI discomfort, and paradoxically reduced nutrient absorption. A modest surplus ensures calories are actually being used rather than causing digestive stress. Additionally, a large surplus will add fat tissue faster than lean tissue can be rebuilt, which is not the goal here.

**Caloric target: 2,900–3,000 kcal per day**

This represents approximately 250–350 kcal above estimated maintenance — enough to support lean tissue rebuilding and glycogen replenishment without overwhelming digestive capacity or adding unnecessary fat.

On training days versus rest days, the difference does not need to be dramatic at this stage. A simple approach: **training days sit at the top of the range (3,000 kcal), rest days sit at the bottom (2,900 kcal).** The difference is small enough that rigid tracking is not required — awareness is sufficient.

---

## Step 3 — Macronutrient Targets

### Protein — The Priority Macro

**Target: 2.0–2.2 g per kg bodyweight = 162–178 g per day**

Round to a working target of **170 g daily.**

Protein is the non-negotiable macro during this block. The muscle protein synthetic response to both training and dietary protein is blunted post-illness due to elevated inflammatory markers and residual hormonal disruption. The way to counteract this is not to eat dramatically more protein than normal — there is a ceiling on how much can be used at once — but to **distribute protein consistently across the day** in doses that maximise the synthetic response at each meal.

**Practical protein distribution:**

| Meal | Protein Target | Example Sources |
|---|---|---|
| Breakfast | 35–40 g | 4 eggs + 150 g Greek yoghurt, or protein shake + 3 eggs |
| Lunch | 40–45 g | 180 g chicken breast + 100 g cottage cheese, or 200 g salmon |
| Pre-training snack | 20–25 g | Protein shake, or 200 g Greek yoghurt |
| Post-training meal | 40–45 g | 200 g lean beef or chicken + dairy source |
| Evening | 25–30 g | Casein shake, or 200 g cottage cheese |

**Total: approximately 160–185 g** — sits comfortably within target.

The pre-sleep protein serving deserves specific mention. Casein protein or cottage cheese before bed has good evidence for supporting overnight muscle protein synthesis, which is particularly relevant during a reconditioning phase when the body is doing significant repair work during sleep. This is not a bro-science recommendation — it is a practical application of well-replicated research.

**Protein sources to prioritise:**
Lean meats (chicken, turkey, lean beef), fish (particularly oily fish for the anti-inflammatory omega-3 benefit), eggs, dairy (Greek yoghurt, cottage cheese, milk), and whey or casein protein supplements as needed to hit targets without excessive food volume.

---

### Carbohydrates — Glycogen Replenishment and Training Fuel

**Target: 4.0–4.5 g per kg bodyweight = 324–364 g per day**

Round to a working target of **340 g daily.**

Carbohydrates are the second priority macro during reconditioning, and arguably the most important for subjective energy levels and training quality. Glycogen depletion is a major contributor to the persistent fatigue he is experiencing — the muscles and liver are running on reduced stores, and the brain is sensitive to this. Adequate carbohydrate intake will produce a noticeable improvement in energy and mood within three to five days, which is important for adherence and motivation.

**Carbohydrate timing matters more than total amount:**

| Timing | Amount | Purpose | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| 60–90 min pre-training | 50–70 g | Top up liver glycogen, sustain training quality | Oats, banana, rice cakes, white bread + jam |
| Within 60 min post-training | 60–80 g | Initiate muscle glycogen resynthesis | White rice, potato, fruit, sports drink if appetite is low |
| Remaining carbs | Distributed across other meals | Sustained energy, micronutrient delivery | Whole grains, vegetables, fruit, legumes |

**Why white/fast carbohydrates around training?**
Post-training, insulin sensitivity in muscle tissue is elevated and glycogen synthase activity is high. This is the window where carbohydrates are most efficiently directed into muscle glycogen rather than fat storage. Fast-digesting carbohydrates exploit this window more effectively than slow-digesting ones. Outside of training windows, whole food carbohydrate sources are preferable for satiety, fibre, and micronutrient content.

**Carbohydrate sources to prioritise:**
Oats, rice (white around training, brown at other meals), potatoes and sweet potatoes, fruit (particularly bananas and berries), whole grain bread, pasta, and legumes. Vegetables contribute carbohydrates and should not be restricted — they also provide the micronutrients and fibre that support immune recovery.

---

### Fat — Hormonal Support and Anti-Inflammatory Function

**Target: 1.0–1.2 g per kg bodyweight = 81–97 g per day**

Round to a working target of **90 g daily.**

Fat is the third macro and the one most commonly either over-restricted or ignored during reconditioning. It deserves attention here for two specific reasons:

**First, testosterone.** Dietary fat is a direct precursor to steroid hormone synthesis. A 41-year-old male who has been ill, lost weight, and is under physical stress will have suppressed testosterone levels. Adequate dietary fat — particularly saturated and monounsaturated fat — supports the restoration of normal testosterone production. This is not the time for an ultra-low-fat diet.

**Second, omega-3 fatty acids.** Post-illness inflammation is still resolving. Omega-3s (EPA and DHA specifically) have well-evidenced anti-inflammatory effects and also support muscle protein synthesis independently of total protein intake. Target **2–3 g of combined EPA and DHA daily**, either through oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines — two to three portions per week) or a high-quality fish oil supplement.

**Fat sources to prioritise:**
Oily fish, eggs (whole eggs, not just whites), olive oil, avocado, nuts and nut butters, full-fat dairy in moderation. Minimise trans fats and heavily processed vegetable oils — these promote rather than resolve inflammation.

## Hydration

**Target: 3.0–3.5 litres of water daily on rest days, 3.5–4.0 litres on training days.**

Hydration is not a secondary consideration here — it is directly tied to the glycogen replenishment process, cognitive function, and cardiovascular efficiency during running. Even mild dehydration of 1–2% of bodyweight measurably impairs both strength output and aerobic performance.

**Electrolytes:**
Plain water is insufficient if he is sweating during training and running. Sodium, potassium, and magnesium all need replacing. Practical options:

- Add a pinch of sea salt to water or meals
- Include potassium-rich foods daily (banana, potato, avocado)
- Consider a basic electrolyte tablet or powder in one water bottle per training day — not a sports drink loaded with sugar, just electrolytes

**Magnesium** deserves a specific mention. It is commonly depleted during illness, plays a role in sleep quality and muscle relaxation, and is frequently under-consumed in Western diets. 300–400 mg of magnesium glycinate or citrate before bed is a reasonable addition and may noticeably improve sleep quality, which is the primary recovery driver during this block.

# Should He Skip Week 1 and Return to Pre-Illness Loads?

## The Short Answer

No. And it is worth being direct with him about why, because "I feel fine today" is one of the most misleading data points in post-illness return to training. The feeling is real — but what it is telling him is incomplete.

---

## Why "I Feel Fine Today" Is Not Sufficient Information

Subjective energy on a given morning reflects a narrow slice of physiology. It captures roughly how well he slept, his current blood glucose, hydration status, and mood. It does not capture any of the following:

**Immune system status.** The inflammatory response to viral illness does not switch off cleanly on the day symptoms resolve. Cytokine activity — the chemical signalling of the immune system — can remain elevated for **two to four weeks post-symptom resolution** in an otherwise healthy adult. Elevated cytokines directly impair muscle protein synthesis, increase perceived exertion at submaximal loads, and slow connective tissue recovery. He cannot feel this. It is happening regardless of his subjective energy report.

**Autonomic nervous system recalibration.** Post-viral autonomic dysfunction is well documented even in mild illness. The balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic activity is disrupted, which means his heart rate response to exercise, his recovery between sets, and his ability to generate maximal neural drive are all likely still below baseline. Again, this is invisible on a good morning. It shows up under load.

**Connective tissue readiness.** Tendons, ligaments, and the connective tissue matrix around muscle fibres adapt more slowly than the muscle itself and are more slowly affected by detraining — but they are also more slowly restored. Three weeks of inactivity means the connective tissue has not been under meaningful load. Jumping to 100 kg on bench, 140 kg on squat, and 170 kg on deadlift on the first session back places full pre-illness mechanical stress on tissue that has had three weeks of reduced loading stimulus. The muscle may handle it. The tendons are a different conversation.

**Glycogen status.** Unless he has been eating well throughout his illness — which most people do not, because illness suppresses appetite — his muscle glycogen stores are likely still partially depleted. He will feel fine warming up. He may feel fine through the first working set. By the third or fourth set at pre-illness loads, he will be drawing on reserves that are not fully stocked. This is where form breaks down and injury risk spikes.

---

## What the Research Actually Says

The science on return to sport after viral illness is fairly consistent on a few points that are directly relevant here:

**Strength loss after three weeks of detraining in a trained individual** is typically in the range of **5–10% of 1RM**, with neural factors accounting for most of the early loss. This means his true current 1RM is probably closer to 90–95 kg on bench, 126–133 kg on squat, and 153–161 kg on deadlift. His pre-illness working loads are not his current working loads. They are loads that exceed his current actual maximum in some cases.

**Post-viral fatigue has a delayed presentation pattern.** This is the critical one. The most common clinical picture is not an athlete who feels terrible and trains anyway. It is an athlete who feels fine, trains hard, feels fine that evening, and then crashes one to three days later with disproportionate fatigue, elevated resting heart rate, disrupted sleep, and prolonged muscle soreness. This pattern is so consistent in the sports medicine literature that it has its own informal name — the **post-exertional rebound.** It is not dangerous in the way myocarditis is dangerous, but it reliably sets recovery back by one to two weeks and is entirely avoidable.

**The two-minute rule in return-to-sport protocols** — used widely in rugby, football, and military contexts — states that an athlete should be able to perform two minutes of moderate aerobic activity without symptoms before returning to any structured training. He passes that test. But those same protocols then prescribe a **graduated return over a minimum of one week** before full training loads are resumed, even for athletes who feel completely well. This is not excessive caution. It is the evidence base.

---

## The Specific Risks at Pre-Illness Loads This Week

Let's be concrete about what could go wrong, because abstract caution is less persuasive than specific scenarios.

**Bench press at 100 kg:** His pec tendons, anterior deltoid, and rotator cuff have not been under meaningful load for three weeks. The neural drive to stabilise the shoulder under a maximal-adjacent load will be reduced. The most likely outcome if something goes wrong is not a dramatic acute injury — it is a low-grade rotator cuff strain that nags for six to eight weeks and limits pressing throughout his entire return programme. The irony is that trying to skip one week of light work could cost him two months of full pressing capacity.

**Squat at 140 kg:** The posterior chain — glutes, hamstrings, spinal erectors — will fatigue faster than his pre-illness baseline under this load. The squat is the lift most sensitive to fatigue-related form breakdown because the consequences of losing position under a heavy bar are significant. A fatigued set at 140 kg where he loses lumbar position in the hole is a lower back injury waiting to happen. Not certain. But the risk-reward calculation is poor.

**Deadlift at 170 kg:** This is the one to be most firm about. The deadlift at near-maximal loads is the highest systemic demand lift in his programme. It taxes the CNS, the posterior chain, the grip, and the cardiovascular system simultaneously. Attempting 170 kg in the first session back after three weeks of illness-related inactivity is genuinely inadvisable. If he grinds it, the recovery cost will be disproportionate. If he fails it, the psychological impact on his return to training is significant. If he strains something, the programme stops entirely.

---

## The Argument He Is Probably Making (And Why It Does Not Hold)

He is likely reasoning something like this: *"I'm an intermediate lifter. I know my body. I've trained through worse. Three weeks isn't that long. I don't want to waste time on baby weights."*

Each of those points has some validity in isolation. He does know his body better than most. Three weeks is not catastrophic detraining. And light loads can feel psychologically deflating for someone who was moving serious weight before illness.

But the reasoning has a flaw at its centre: **he is using pre-illness self-knowledge to make a post-illness decision.** His body right now is not the same body that benched 100 kg three weeks ago. It has been through a systemic viral illness, lost 4 kg, been sedentary for three weeks, and is still completing its immune recovery. The self-knowledge he is drawing on does not apply to his current physiological state.

The "I've trained through worse" instinct is also worth examining. Training through fatigue during a normal training block is a skill. Training through post-viral fatigue is a different thing entirely — it is overriding a genuine physiological signal, not just a psychological one.

---

## What You Should Tell Him

Be straightforward. Something like:

*"I hear you, and I believe you feel good today. That's genuinely a positive sign. But feeling good this morning doesn't tell us what your tendons, your nervous system, and your immune system are doing — and those are the things that get damaged if we rush this. The week of lighter work isn't because I doubt your fitness. It's because I want you back at your real numbers in three weeks, not stuck at 60% for six weeks because something went wrong on day one. One week of smart work is the fastest route to where you want to be."*

If he pushes back further, offer him this concrete test: **do Week 1 Session 1A exactly as prescribed, at the prescribed loads, with the prescribed tempo.** If he walks out of that session feeling like it was genuinely too easy and recovers perfectly over the following 48 hours with no unusual fatigue or soreness, you can have a conversation about compressing the timeline slightly in Week 2. But the data from that first session — how his body actually responds under load, not how he feels before it — is the information you need before making any programming decisions.

---

## The Bottom Line

Feeling fine is a necessary condition for returning to training. It is not a sufficient condition for returning to pre-illness loads. The week of reconditioning work is not a punishment or an insult to his fitness level. It is the mechanism by which he gets back to 100 kg / 140 kg / 170 kg in three weeks rather than in three months. The risk of skipping it is asymmetric — the upside is saving one week, the downside is a setback of four to eight weeks. That is not a trade worth making.

# Readiness Signals for Return to Full Intensity

## The Core Problem With Readiness Assessment

Most athletes — and many trainers — treat readiness as a binary. Either you're ready or you're not. In reality it is a **convergence of signals** across multiple physiological and psychological systems, and the decision to return to full intensity should be based on that convergence, not on any single indicator. One good night's sleep does not mean he is ready. One strong session does not mean he is ready. What you are looking for is **consistent positive signals across all the domains below, sustained over multiple days.**

The other important framing: readiness for full intensity is not the same as readiness to train. He has been ready to train since Week 1 began. Full intensity means pre-illness loads, pre-illness volume, pre-illness training density, and pre-illness running pace. That is a higher bar and it requires more evidence.

---

## Domain 1 — Resting Heart Rate

This is the single most objective and accessible physiological readiness marker available without lab testing.

**What to do:** Have him measure resting heart rate first thing in the morning, before getting out of bed, every day throughout the reconditioning block. A chest strap or reliable wrist monitor is preferable to a manual count for consistency. After three to four days of measurement you will establish his current baseline.

**What you are looking for:** Resting HR that is **within 3–5 bpm of his established pre-illness baseline.** If he does not know his pre-illness resting HR, use the average of Days 3–7 of the reconditioning block as a proxy baseline, once acute recovery is underway.

**What elevated resting HR tells you:** The heart rate is controlled by the autonomic nervous system. Persistent elevation — even 6–8 bpm above baseline — indicates the sympathetic nervous system is still dominant, meaning the body is still in a physiological stress state. Training at full intensity in this state adds load to a system that is already working hard. It does not accelerate recovery. It competes with it.

**The number to act on:** If resting HR is consistently within normal range for five or more consecutive mornings, this domain is cleared. If it spikes on any given morning — even after what felt like a good training day — treat that as a yellow flag and do not increase intensity that week.

---

## Domain 2 — Sleep Quality and Duration

Sleep is where adaptation happens. It is also the most sensitive early warning system for inadequate recovery.

**What you are looking for:**
- Falling asleep within 20–30 minutes of going to bed without difficulty
- Sleeping 7–9 hours without frequent waking
- Waking feeling genuinely refreshed rather than still tired
- No need for alarm-dependent waking — waking naturally near a consistent time

**Why this matters specifically post-illness:** Viral illness disrupts the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, which regulates both the stress response and sleep architecture. Deep slow-wave sleep — the stage most associated with physical recovery and growth hormone release — is often the last thing to fully normalise after illness. An athlete can be sleeping eight hours and still not getting adequate restorative sleep if the architecture is disrupted. The subjective experience of waking refreshed is therefore more informative than hours alone.

**The signal to look for:** At least five to seven consecutive nights of good quality sleep, with subjective morning freshness consistently at 7 out of 10 or above. A single bad night is not disqualifying — life happens. A pattern of poor sleep is a hard stop on intensity progression.

---

## Domain 3 — Training Performance Trajectory

This is the most direct evidence of physiological readiness and the one you have the most control over as a trainer.

**What you are looking for across the reconditioning block:**

**Bar speed.** At any given percentage of 1RM, bar speed is a proxy for neural drive and muscular readiness. As he recovers, bar speed at the prescribed loads should increase week on week. If 70 kg squats in Week 1 move slowly and 84 kg squats in Week 2 move at the same speed or faster, that is a positive readiness signal. If bar speed is not improving — or worse, is declining — the system is not recovering adequately.

**Perceived exertion versus actual load.** An RPE of 6–7 at 70% of pre-illness 1RM in Week 3 is a strong readiness signal. An RPE of 8–9 at the same load is a signal to wait. The gap between how hard the load feels and how hard it should feel is one of the most informative data points you can collect.

**Recovery between sets.** Is he recovering fully within the prescribed rest periods? Post-illness, cardiovascular recovery between sets is often slower than normal even when the lift itself feels manageable. If he needs significantly more than the prescribed rest to feel ready for the next set, the system is not yet at full capacity.

**Session-to-session freshness.** Is he arriving at each session feeling ready to train, or is he carrying fatigue from the previous session? At full readiness, an intermediate lifter should recover from a moderate training session within 24–36 hours. If soreness or fatigue is persisting beyond 48 hours consistently, he is not ready for full intensity.

**The specific benchmark for the three primary lifts:** By the end of Week 3, if he is completing 4 sets of 5 reps at 70–75% with good bar speed, clean technique, RPE of 6–7, and recovering well between sessions, the physiological case for returning to full intensity in Week 4 is strong.

---

## Domain 4 — Subjective Energy and Mood

This is the domain he has already been reporting on — and as discussed, it is necessary but not sufficient on its own. However, tracked consistently and honestly, it provides genuinely useful information.

**What to track:** Ask him to score the following each morning on a simple 1–10 scale. Keep it quick — if it takes more than 30 seconds he will stop doing it.

- Overall energy
- Motivation to train
- Muscle soreness
- Mood

**What you are looking for:** A consistent upward trend across all four markers over the three-week block. Not perfection — a 7 or 8 across the board, sustained, is the target. Specifically:

**Energy at 7+ consistently** means the adrenal and metabolic systems are functioning normally. Post-illness fatigue characteristically produces energy scores of 4–6 even on good days — when he is consistently hitting 7–8 without a significant dip after training sessions, that is a meaningful signal.

**Motivation at 7+** is worth paying attention to because low motivation in a previously motivated athlete is often a physiological signal, not a psychological one. Chronically low motivation during recovery frequently reflects elevated cortisol and suppressed testosterone — the hormonal environment of incomplete recovery. When motivation returns strongly and consistently, it often reflects normalising hormone levels.

**Soreness below 4** after training sessions that would previously have produced minimal soreness is a readiness signal. Disproportionate soreness from moderate loads indicates the inflammatory response is still heightened.

**The pattern to watch for:** A spike in any of these scores after a training session — energy crashing, mood dropping, soreness spiking — is a post-exertional signal that the load exceeded current recovery capacity. One instance is a data point. Two instances in a week is a clear message to hold intensity where it is.

---

## Domain 5 — Bodyweight Trajectory

Weight alone means little. Weight in context means quite a lot.

**What you are looking for:**

**Consistent upward trend** from his current 81 kg back toward his pre-illness 85 kg. As outlined in the nutrition section, the first 1.5–2 kg will return quickly from glycogen and water. After that, genuine lean tissue rebuilding should produce a slow, steady increase of 0.3–0.5 kg per week.

**Stability around a new baseline.** Bodyweight that is fluctuating wildly day to day — more than 1.5–2 kg of daily variation beyond normal hydration fluctuation — suggests the metabolic and hormonal environment is still unsettled.

**The specific signal:** When bodyweight has been stable or trending upward for two consecutive weeks and is within 1–2 kg of pre-illness weight, the nutritional and metabolic recovery is largely complete. This is a supporting signal for readiness, not a standalone one.

---

## Domain 6 — Running-Specific Readiness

Given his 10k background, running provides an additional and highly sensitive readiness window that lifting alone does not.

**Heart rate at a given pace.** This is the most objective running readiness marker. As he recovers, his heart rate at any given pace should decrease week on week. If he ran at 7:00 per kilometre at 128 bpm in Week 1 and is running the same pace at 118 bpm in Week 3, that is measurable cardiovascular recovery. When his heart rate at easy pace returns to within **5–8 bpm of his pre-illness easy run HR**, cardiovascular readiness is largely restored.

**Pace at a given heart rate.** The inverse of the above — at a fixed heart rate ceiling of 130 bpm, his pace should be getting faster week on week. When he can hold his pre-illness easy pace at or below his pre-illness easy run heart rate, the aerobic system has recovered.

**Post-run recovery.** How does he feel in the 24–48 hours after a run? A fully recovered athlete should feel minimal fatigue the day after an easy run. If runs are producing disproportionate fatigue or soreness, the cardiovascular system is still under stress.

**The specific benchmark:** When he can complete a 40–45 minute easy run at his pre-illness easy pace without his heart rate drifting above 140 bpm, and recovers normally within 24 hours, running readiness is confirmed.

---

## Domain 7 — The 48-Hour Post-Session Response

This deserves its own section because it is the most important single readiness test and the one most commonly ignored.

**The principle:** How an athlete feels during a session tells you relatively little. How they feel 24–48 hours after a session tells you almost everything about whether the load was appropriate for their current recovery capacity.

**What full readiness looks like post-session:**
- Mild muscle soreness that peaks at 24 hours and is largely resolved by 48 hours
- Energy levels that return to baseline or above within 24 hours
- Sleep quality unaffected or improved the night after training
- Motivation to train maintained or increased
- Resting heart rate stable or slightly elevated the morning after, returning to baseline by 48 hours

**What incomplete readiness looks like post-session:**
- Soreness that is still significant at 48–72 hours
- Energy that crashes the day after training and does not recover quickly
- Sleep disruption the night after a hard session
- Motivation that drops noticeably after training
- Resting heart rate that remains elevated for more than 48 hours post-session

**Why this matters for the full intensity decision:** The post-exertional rebound pattern described earlier — feeling fine, training hard, crashing two days later — is caught entirely by this 48-hour monitoring window. If he completes Week 3 sessions at 70–75% and the 48-hour response is clean across all three sessions, that is strong evidence the system can handle full intensity. If any session produces a disproportionate 48-hour response, the answer is another week at current loads.

---

## Pulling It Together — The Readiness Checklist

Before clearing him for full pre-illness loads, you want to be able to tick every box on this list:

**Objective markers:**
- [ ] Resting HR within 3–5 bpm of baseline for 5+ consecutive mornings
- [ ] Bodyweight within 1–2 kg of pre-illness weight and stable or trending up
- [ ] Bar speed improving week on week at prescribed loads
- [ ] Running HR at easy pace within 5–8 bpm of pre-illness baseline
- [ ] 48-hour post-session response clean across all Week 3 sessions

**Subjective markers:**
- [ ] Morning energy consistently 7+ for 5+ consecutive days
- [ ] Motivation to train consistently 7+ 
- [ ] Post-session soreness resolving within 48 hours
- [ ] Sleep quality consistently good — falling asleep easily, waking refreshed
- [ ] No post-exertional energy crashes after any Week 3 session

**Performance markers:**
- [ ] Completing all prescribed sets and reps at Week 3 loads with good technique
- [ ] RPE at 70–75% loads sitting at 6–7, not 8–9
- [ ] Recovering fully between sets within prescribed rest periods
- [ ] Arriving at each session feeling fresh from the previous one

**The decision rule:** If all three categories are green, clear him for full intensity in Week 4 at 80–85% of pre-illness loads — not 100%, but a confident step toward it. If any category has amber or red signals, extend the reconditioning block by one week and reassess. There is no circumstance in which a single strong session overrides persistent amber signals elsewhere.

---

## One Final Point

The readiness conversation is also a coaching conversation. An athlete who understands why these signals matter — who has bought into the monitoring process rather than just tolerating it — will give you more accurate self-reports and will be less likely to push past genuine warning signs. 

The framing that tends to work: **these signals are not gatekeeping his training. They are the map that gets him back to full intensity as fast as safely possible.** Every time the signals are green and you advance the programme, that is the monitoring system working. Every time a signal catches a problem before it becomes an injury or a setback, that is the monitoring system earning its place. The goal is not caution for its own sake. It is the fastest legitimate route back to 100 kg, 140 kg, and 170 kg — and beyond.

# 1RM Testing Protocol — Week 3

## Should We Actually Test 1RM at the End of Week 3?

Before building the protocol, this recommendation needs to be examined honestly, because it sits in some tension with everything the reconditioning block has been designed around. A 1RM test is a maximal effort by definition — it is the highest possible load on the nervous system, the connective tissue, and the musculoskeletal system. The question is whether the end of Week 3 is the right moment for that, or whether it creates a risk that outweighs the benefit of having precise numbers.

**The case for testing:**
Real numbers produce better programming. Percentage-based programming off estimated or pre-illness 1RMs is always an approximation, and after illness and detraining that approximation carries more error than usual. If his squat has come back to 130 kg but you programme Week 4 off 140 kg, every percentage in the new block is wrong. A genuine 1RM test eliminates that uncertainty and gives the returning programme a solid foundation.

**The case against testing at the end of Week 3:**
Three weeks of reconditioning work, even well-executed, is not the same as three weeks of genuine strength training. The body has been re-sensitised and progressively loaded, but it has not been specifically prepared for maximal effort. A true 1RM attempt requires not just physical readiness but neural readiness — the ability to recruit maximum motor units under a genuinely heavy load. That quality takes longer to restore than general training capacity.

**The resolution:**
Test, but do not treat it as a true 1RM in the classical sense. What we are running at the end of Week 3 is better described as a **conservative estimated maximum protocol** — a structured, carefully ramped session that finds a heavy single that he completes with good technique and without maximal grinding, then uses that number to back-calculate a working 1RM estimate. This gives you real, current numbers to programme from without asking the system to produce a genuine all-out effort before it is fully ready for one.

The distinction matters practically: a true 1RM attempt involves grinding through sticking points, maximal bracing, and complete neural recruitment. What we are doing is finding the heaviest load he can lift **cleanly and confidently** — which will be slightly below his true current maximum, and that is intentional. The programming that follows will be more accurate and safer for it.

---

## Timing Within Week 3

The test does not replace Week 3 sessions. It replaces Session 3C — the full body session that already contained all three primary lifts. This is deliberate: Session 3C was already structured as a mini full-body assessment, so the testing session is a natural evolution of that intent rather than an addition to the week's load.

**Revised Week 3 Schedule:**

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Session 3A — Lower Body / Squat Focus (as programmed) |
| Tuesday | Run 3 — 35–40 min easy, HR ≤ 140 bpm |
| Wednesday | Session 3B — Upper Body / Bench Focus (as programmed) |
| Thursday | Full rest — no running, no gym, no active recovery beyond walking |
| Friday | **1RM Assessment Session** |
| Saturday | Light active recovery — walking only |
| Sunday | Full rest |

**Why Thursday is full rest:**
This is non-negotiable. The assessment session requires the nervous system to be as fresh as possible. A run or active recovery session on Thursday would blunt neural readiness on Friday in a way that meaningfully affects the numbers produced. One full rest day between Session 3B and the assessment is the minimum. If the client's schedule allows two rest days before the assessment — moving it to Saturday — that is preferable.

---

## Pre-Assessment Requirements

Before the session begins, confirm the following. If any of these are not met, postpone the assessment by one week and continue at Week 3 loads.

**Physical readiness checklist — confirm on Thursday evening and Friday morning:**
- Resting heart rate within normal range — within 3–5 bpm of his reconditioning baseline
- No significant muscle soreness from Session 3B — mild stiffness is acceptable, genuine soreness is not
- Sleep of 7+ hours on both Wednesday and Thursday nights
- No illness symptoms of any kind — even mild
- Morning energy score of 7 or above on Friday
- Well hydrated — urine pale yellow, not dark
- No alcohol in the preceding 48 hours
- A proper meal containing carbohydrates and protein two to three hours before the session

If he arrives on Friday morning reporting poor sleep, elevated soreness, or energy below 6, postpone. The numbers produced in a suboptimal state are not useful numbers — they will underestimate his true current capacity and produce a programme that is too conservative. Better data comes from a better day.

---

## Session Structure

**Total session duration: approximately 75–90 minutes.** Longer than normal sessions but justified by the warm-up requirements of maximal lifting. Do not rush the warm-up to save time — the warm-up is where injury prevention happens in a testing session.

**Order of lifts:** Squat first, bench second, deadlift third. This is the conventional powerlifting competition order and it exists for good reasons — the squat is the most technically demanding and benefits most from a fully warm nervous system, while the deadlift is the most systemically fatiguing and should come last so it does not compromise the other two.

**Rest between lifts:** Minimum 10–12 minutes between completing the final attempt on one lift and beginning the warm-up sets for the next. Use this time for light movement, hydration, and mental preparation — not sitting down and going cold.

---

## The Warm-Up Protocol

The warm-up for a testing session is more structured and more important than a normal session warm-up. It serves three purposes: raising tissue temperature, progressively loading the nervous system toward maximal recruitment, and providing information about how the body is responding before heavy loads are attempted.

**General warm-up — 10 minutes:**
- 5 minutes easy cycling or rowing — HR to approximately 120–125 bpm
- World's greatest stretch — 5 reps each side
- Hip 90/90 rotations — 5 each side
- Thoracic rotation in quadruped — 8 each side
- Band pull-aparts — 2 × 20
- Glute bridges — 2 × 15
- Scapular push-ups — 2 × 10

This is not optional and should not be abbreviated. A 41-year-old post-illness athlete attempting near-maximal loads without a thorough warm-up is an injury risk regardless of how good he feels.

---

## Lift 1 — Squat

### Warm-Up Sets

| Set | Load | Reps | Rest After |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 20 kg (empty bar) | 8 | 90 sec |
| 2 | 40 kg | 5 | 90 sec |
| 3 | 60 kg | 3 | 2 min |
| 4 | 80 kg | 2 | 2.5 min |
| 5 | 95 kg | 1 | 3 min |
| 6 | 107 kg | 1 | 3.5 min |

### Working Attempts

| Attempt | Load | Target | Rest After |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attempt 1 | **115 kg** | Confident single, RPE 7–8 | 4 min |
| Attempt 2 | **122–125 kg** | Based on Attempt 1 quality | 5 min |
| Attempt 3 | **128–132 kg** | Only if Attempt 2 was clean and fast | 5 min |

**Decision rules between attempts:**

After Attempt 1 at 115 kg, assess the following before loading Attempt 2:
- Did it move with reasonable bar speed through the sticking point?
- Was technique clean — depth achieved, no excessive forward lean, no knee cave?
- RPE — did it feel like a 7–8, or was it already a 9?

If Attempt 1 was clean and RPE was 7–8, load to 122–125 kg for Attempt 2.
If Attempt 1 was slow or technically compromised, stop at 115 kg. That is today's number.

After Attempt 2, apply the same logic. If it moved well and RPE was 8 or below, a third attempt at 128–132 kg is reasonable. If it was a grind — slow bar speed, significant struggle through the sticking point, RPE 9 — stop at Attempt 2. A grinding rep at this stage of reconditioning is not a number to programme from. It is a number that will produce overreaching in Week 4.

**Maximum three attempts.** No fourth attempts regardless of how he feels. The fatigue accumulation from three heavy singles is already significant and the deadlift is still to come.

**Estimated 1RM calculation:**
Use the Epley formula as a cross-check: **(weight × reps × 0.0333) + weight.** For a single rep this simply returns the weight lifted, but if you stop at a double on any attempt you can use it to estimate the single equivalent. More usefully, if his best clean single is 125 kg, apply a **conservative 1.05–1.08 multiplier** to estimate his true 1RM — giving approximately 131–135 kg. Use the lower end for programming.

---

## Lift 2 — Bench Press

**Rest 10–12 minutes after completing squat attempts before beginning bench warm-up.**

### Warm-Up Sets

| Set | Load | Reps | Rest After |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 20 kg (empty bar) | 8 | 90 sec |
| 2 | 40 kg | 5 | 90 sec |
| 3 | 55 kg | 3 | 2 min |
| 4 | 67 kg | 2 | 2.5 min |
| 5 | 77 kg | 1 | 3 min |

### Working Attempts

| Attempt | Load | Target | Rest After |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attempt 1 | **82–85 kg** | Confident single, RPE 7–8 | 4 min |
| Attempt 2 | **88–90 kg** | Based on Attempt 1 quality | 5 min |
| Attempt 3 | **93–95 kg** | Only if Attempt 2 was clean and fast | 5 min |

**Decision rules between attempts:**

The bench press is the lift where post-illness shoulder health is most likely to be a limiting factor. Watch specifically for:
- Any asymmetry in the press — one side lagging or the bar tilting
- Shoulder discomfort at the bottom of the range of motion
- Excessive elbow flare indicating anterior deltoid compensation
- Bar path drifting toward the face rather than tracking back over the shoulder

Any of these is a reason to stop at the current attempt regardless of the load. A shoulder issue caught here is a minor inconvenience. A shoulder issue that develops because you pushed through warning signs is a six-week setback.

If Attempt 1 at 82–85 kg is clean and RPE is 7–8, advance to 88–90 kg. If Attempt 2 is clean and RPE is 8 or below, a third attempt at 93–95 kg is reasonable. His pre-illness 1RM was 100 kg — a clean single at 93–95 kg at this stage of reconditioning is an excellent result and gives you a solid number to programme from.

**Estimated 1RM:** Apply the same 1.05–1.08 multiplier to his best clean single. A 92 kg clean single estimates to approximately 97–99 kg true 1RM. Programme from the lower end.

---

## Lift 3 — Deadlift

**Rest 10–12 minutes after completing bench attempts before beginning deadlift warm-up. This rest period is more important here than on the other lifts — the deadlift is the most systemically demanding and the nervous system will be accumulating fatigue from the squat and bench work.**

### Warm-Up Sets

| Set | Load | Reps | Rest After |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 60 kg | 5 | 90 sec |
| 2 | 80 kg | 3 | 2 min |
| 3 | 100 kg | 2 | 2.5 min |
| 4 | 120 kg | 1 | 3 min |
| 5 | 135 kg | 1 | 3.5 min |

### Working Attempts

| Attempt | Load | Target | Rest After |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attempt 1 | **142–145 kg** | Confident single, RPE 7–8 | 5 min |
| Attempt 2 | **150–153 kg** | Based on Attempt 1 quality | 5–6 min |
| Attempt 3 | **157–160 kg** | Only if Attempt 2 was genuinely clean | 5–6 min |

**Decision rules between attempts:**

The deadlift decision rules are the strictest of the three lifts because the consequences of a failed or technically compromised heavy deadlift are the most significant.

After Attempt 1, assess:
- Did the bar break the floor cleanly without hitching or excessive hip rise?
- Was the lower back position maintained throughout — no rounding at the top of the pull?
- Was lockout clean and controlled?
- RPE — 7–8 or already pushing 9?

**Be particularly conservative here.** By the time he reaches the deadlift, he has already completed six to nine heavy singles across the squat and bench. Neural fatigue is real and it affects the deadlift more than the other two lifts. A load that would have been an RPE 7 fresh may be an RPE 8.5 at this point in the session. Factor that in when making jump decisions.

If there is any lower back fatigue or tightness from the squat work, stop the deadlift at Attempt 1 regardless of the load. The lower back is the structure you are most protecting in this entire reconditioning block. It is not worth a third deadlift attempt to get a slightly more precise number.

**Estimated 1RM:** Apply the same 1.05–1.08 multiplier. A clean single at 152 kg estimates to approximately 160–164 kg true 1RM. Programme from the lower end.

---

## Recording the Results

After the session, record the following for each lift:

| Lift | Best Clean Single | Estimated 1RM | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Squat | ___ kg | ___ kg | Technique observations |
| Bench | ___ kg | ___ kg | Technique observations |
| Deadlift | ___ kg | ___ kg | Technique observations |

The technique observations column is not optional. The numbers tell you where he is. The technique notes tell you what to prioritise in the programme that follows. If the squat showed a consistent forward lean at depth, that is a cue for the next programming block. If the bench showed shoulder asymmetry, that flags accessory work priorities. The testing session is diagnostic as well as numerical.

---

## Expected Results and What They Mean

Based on the detraining and reconditioning trajectory, here is a realistic expectation of where his estimated 1RMs should land after three weeks of this block:

| Lift | Pre-Illness 1RM | Expected Post-Reconditioning Estimated 1RM | % of Baseline |
|---|---|---|---|
| Squat | 140 kg | 128–135 kg | 91–96% |
| Bench | 100 kg | 90–96 kg | 90–96% |
| Deadlift | 170 kg | 155–163 kg | 91–96% |

If his results land within these ranges, the reconditioning block has done exactly what it was designed to do and the programme transition is straightforward. If results are significantly below these ranges — more than 10% below pre-illness 1RM — that is a signal that recovery is taking longer than expected and the subsequent programme should be more conservative than planned. If results are at or above the top of these ranges, he has recovered faster than average and you can be slightly more aggressive with the opening loads in the new programme.

---

## Using the Numbers — Resetting the Programme

Once you have estimated 1RMs from the testing session, the new programme opens at **80% of those estimated 1RMs**, not 80% of his pre-illness numbers. This is the critical point. The testing session gives you his current baseline. That is the number everything is built from.

**Example using mid-range expected results:**

| Lift | Estimated 1RM from Test | Week 4 Opening Load (80%) |
|---|---|---|
| Squat | 132 kg | 105 kg |
| Bench | 93 kg | 74 kg |
| Deadlift | 159 kg | 127 kg |

From these opening loads, a standard linear or undulating progression will return him to his pre-illness 1RMs within **three to five weeks**, and should take him beyond them within **eight to ten weeks** — assuming nutrition, sleep, and training consistency are maintained. The reconditioning block plus the testing session has not cost him time. It has given him a precise, safe launchpad for the strongest programming block he has had in months.

|---|---|
